title: One master, a thousand disks
teaches: Splitting metadata from data, big blocks, and why one coordinator can be the right first design
summary: **GFS was built for one kind of file.** A few million files of many megabytes to many gigabytes, written by appending and read in long streams, on a thousand cheap machines.
**Metadata and data take different paths.** One master knows every file's chunks and where they are; the bytes go straight between clients and chunkservers.

**The master's tables live in memory.** The master holds the file namespace, each file's list of chunks, and each chunk's replica locations in RAM, rebuilding the location map at startup by polling the chunkservers.
**Big chunks keep the master small and quiet.** At 64 MB a chunk and under 64 bytes each, a petabyte is about 16 million chunks and 1 GB of memory, and a client asks the master once per chunk.
**Big chunks cost something too.** A small file sits in one chunk on three machines, and if many clients want it at once those three become a hot spot.
**One coordinator makes global decisions simple.** Placement, re-replication and garbage collection are decided in one place with all the facts, as long as its load and memory stay small.
**The master's state survives in a replicated log.** Every change to names and chunk lists is written to an operation log copied to other machines before the client is told it is done.
**Know where the simple design stops.** By 2009 file counts and latency-sensitive users had outgrown one master, and Google replaced GFS with Colossus, which spreads the metadata.

blocks.text: In 1999 Google's servers were bare circuit boards, several to a shelf. The company bought the cheapest machines that would do, in large numbers, and accepted that some of them would always be broken. We look at that choice in Lesson 7. In this lesson, we examine the file system it led to.

Google's work was dominated by a few enormous jobs. A crawler fetched billions of web pages and wrote them to files; programs read those files from start to finish to build the search index; logs of every search piled up to be read the same way. No single disk could hold the data, and no file system of the time would spread one file system's worth of files over a thousand machines. In October 2003 Sanjay Ghemawat, Howard Gobioff and Shun-Tak Leung published how they had built one, "The Google File System".[^authors] Its largest clusters then held hundreds of terabytes over more than a thousand machines.

The design surprised readers. At the centre of a file system spread over a thousand machines sat a single machine, the **master**, that knew where everything was. Many people's first thought was that it must be a bottleneck and a single point of failure. The paper's authors had thought about both. In this lesson, we will look at why the master was neither for the workload it was built to serve, and at the point where that stopped being true.

The authors began the paper by describing the workload the system was built for, and those requirements drove the design. Files were large: a few million of them, typically 100 MB or more, with many reaching several gigabytes. Most were changed by **appending** to the end, often by many programs at once, and were almost never overwritten in the middle. Most reads were long sequential streams through a file from start to finish, while a few were small reads at random offsets. Steady throughput of many megabytes a second for hours mattered more than the latency of any single read.

What the designers left out was just as important. Small files worked, but they were not efficient. The file system did not offer a POSIX interface, the standard set of file operations and guarantees that Unix programs are written against, so ordinary programs could not use it unchanged. Low latency for small reads was not a goal. Each omission made the design simpler, and each became a bottleneck when later teams used the system differently. Deciding what a system will not support is as much an engineering choice as deciding what it will.

GFS divides every file into **chunks** of 64 MB, each identified by a 64-bit number called its chunk handle. Each chunk is stored as an ordinary Linux file on three different **chunkservers**, the machines with the disks. The master keeps the **metadata**, which is the data about the data, consisting of the file namespace, the list of chunks in each file, and the locations of each chunk's replicas.

blocks.caption: What the master keeps in memory, and what is on the chunkservers. The master never holds file contents.

blocks.text: Reading a file takes two steps. The client converts the byte offset it wants into a chunk index (dividing the offset by 64 MB) and asks the master for that chunk's handle and replica locations. Then it requests the bytes directly from the nearest chunkserver. The master sits on the **control path**, tracking and deciding where chunks live; the bytes travel on the **data path**, straight from chunkserver to client, without touching the master. The client caches the master's reply, so a program streaming through a 64 MB chunk in 1 MB reads queries the master once and the chunkserver 64 times.[^cache]

blocks.caption: Clients reading 10 GB a second in 1 MB pieces, with a master assumed to answer 2,000 requests a second, a made-up round number for the figure. Slow motion, at a small fraction of the rate.
blocks.task: Shrink the chunks, or send the data through the master, until the master is the box that is full.

blocks.text: We can check the numbers before trusting a single master. Clients reading 10 GB a second in 1 MB pieces make 10,000 reads a second. With 64 MB chunks they send about 160 requests a second to the master, which is a light load for one machine. With 1 MB chunks the master receives all 10,000 requests a second. If the data also passed through the master, as it would if the coordinator served the bytes itself, one machine's network card would have to carry all 10 GB a second, whereas a gigabit link in 2003 carried only about 0.1 GB a second. Suppose the master can answer 2,000 requests a second (the figure uses this round number, though an engineer would measure a real master's limit). With 64 MB chunks, the master sits at under 10% utilisation. A single master works because it performs one small lookup per chunk rather than per read or per byte, kept small by the 64 MB chunk size and the separate data path.

parts.title: Why the chunks are so big

blocks.text: In 2003, a local file system typically stored files in blocks of 4 KB, and a few used 64 KB. GFS's 64 MB chunk size is 16,384 times larger than 4 KB, chosen to protect the master's memory. The master keeps all its metadata tables in RAM so that every lookup is a fast memory reference and no request waits on a disk read. According to the paper, each chunk requires less than 64 bytes of master memory.

blocks.caption: Master memory for the metadata, at under 64 bytes a block, on a scale where each gridline is a thousand times the last. Guess first.
blocks.task: Guess how much master memory a petabyte of files needs in 64 MB chunks.

blocks.text: A petabyte of data in 64 MB chunks comes to about 16 million chunks. At 64 bytes per chunk, that takes about 1 GB of memory, which fits easily in one ordinary server with room to spare for file names and chunk lists. The same petabyte divided into 4 KB blocks produces 250 billion blocks and requires 16 TB of metadata, which no machine could hold in memory in 2003 and very few can today. The block size determines whether a single machine can track the entire system in RAM. When you choose a chunk size for another storage system, you set a lower bound with two calculations: the total data stored divided by the chunk size, multiplied by the metadata bytes per chunk, must fit in the coordinator's memory, and the client read rate divided by the reads per chunk must stay within the coordinator's request capacity. As an upper bound, the chunk size must remain small enough that a typical file spans several chunks, allowing clients to read it from several machines in parallel.

Large chunks have downsides, which the authors noted in the paper. A file of a few kilobytes still occupies one chunk on three chunkservers. Because the underlying Linux file on disk only uses as much space as the actual data, disk capacity is not wasted, but that file is served by only three machines. When hundreds of client machines read the same small file at the same moment, those three chunkservers become a bottleneck. The authors encountered this when hundreds of machines simultaneously launched an executable binary stored as a small file in GFS; they fixed it by increasing the replication factor for binaries and staggering application start times.[^hotspot] Any design choice that optimises the common case makes some uncommon case more expensive, so engineers must identify which edge cases their system can tolerate.

Beyond being simpler to build, a single master has a major operational advantage because it holds the entire system's state in one place. Choosing where to place a new chunk's replicas depends on every chunkserver's free disk space, current load and rack location, all of which the master already tracks. When a chunkserver fails, the master knows right away which chunks lost a replica and schedules new copies (as we cover in Lesson 7). To clean up deleted files, the master lazily scans its own tables during background garbage collection. Distributing those decisions across multiple coordinators requires those machines to run a distributed consensus protocol to agree on state, which we will see in Lesson 11 is one of the hardest problems in systems engineering. By keeping global state small enough for one coordinator, the builders avoided distributed coordination across the rest of the system.

The master must not lose its metadata tables, so before telling a client that an operation succeeded, the master appends every change to the file namespace or chunk lists to an **operation log** on its local disk and replicates that log entry to remote machines. Periodically, the master writes its complete in-memory state to disk as a checkpoint file; on restart, it loads the latest checkpoint and replays only the subsequent log entries. The master does not log chunk replica locations at all. Instead, it polls every chunkserver at startup to learn what chunks they hold, and updates its map through periodic **heartbeats**, which are short messages each chunkserver sends every few seconds to report its status and inventory. Because each chunkserver is the source of truth for its own disks, the master never has to keep a persistent location database synchronised with the actual drives.

Clients reach the master through a DNS alias rather than a fixed IP address. If the master machine fails, an external monitoring system starts a new master process on another machine using the replicated operation log and updates the DNS record. In the meantime, read-only **shadow masters** that tail the operation log with a slight delay continue serving read metadata to clients. The single master is therefore a single point of failure for write operations during the time it takes to restart, a trade-off the designers accepted because batch processing jobs could easily pause for a minute.

In August 2009 Sean Quinlan, who had led GFS's development, described in a conversation with Kirk McKusick, published in ACM Queue, how the system had been pushed far beyond what it was designed for. Google now stored many more, much smaller files, and the number of files, not their size, was the master's limit: every file costs memory, and some clusters had hundreds of millions of them. Applications such as Gmail wanted answers in milliseconds from a system built for batch jobs that could wait, and a master failover that a batch job hardly noticed was an outage to someone reading their mail.[^quinlan]

Around 2010, Google began replacing GFS with a new file system called Colossus. Colossus stores file metadata as rows in Bigtable (which we cover in Lesson 10), a distributed database that shards tables by key range across many machines; this spreads the file namespace across a cluster of metadata servers rather than holding it on one machine, while the storage layer uses erasure coding (Lesson 7) instead of three full replicas.[^colossus] Building a distributed metadata layer was much more complex, and Google undertook it roughly seven years after publishing the GFS paper, once engineers had hit and measured the limits of a single master. Outside Google, the Hadoop Distributed File System (HDFS) replicated the GFS architecture in 2006 using a single coordinator called the NameNode, and its operators eventually ran into the exact same memory ceiling with small files.

Starting with a single master was a sound engineering decision. It allowed a small team to put a working file system into production quickly, supported Google's storage growth for nearly a decade, and had predictable scaling limits based on simple arithmetic: RAM bytes per file and RPC requests per chunk. When designing your own systems, isolate the coordination logic in a small, simple component, and calculate up front the exact load and capacity numbers at which you will have to replace it.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Control path through the master; data path straight to the chunkservers.
Metadata in memory: a petabyte in 64 MB chunks is about 16 million chunks, and at 64 bytes each about 1 GB.
A single coordinator is fine while its share of the work is small, and its limits can be computed in advance.

blocks.caption: Six questions on the master and its chunks
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Why was GFS's single master not a bottleneck for clients reading gigabytes a second?
choices: It ran on a much larger machine than the chunkservers, with many more disks
Clients asked it only where chunks were, then read from chunkservers
It kept a copy of every popular chunk in memory and served those reads itself
items.why: The master is on the control path only. A client asks once per chunk and caches the answer, so reading 10 GB a second in 1 MB pieces costs the master about 160 requests a second.

items.ask: A GFS master keeps under 64 bytes per 64 MB chunk. About how much memory does it need for 4 PB of files?
items.why: 4 PB / 64 MB is about 62 million chunks; multiplied by 64 bytes, that comes to about 4 GB. In 4 KB blocks the same data would need about 64 TB.

items.ask: What did GFS give up by choosing 64 MB chunks?
choices: Efficient use of disk space, since every small file filled a whole 64 MB on disk
Fast streaming reads, since each chunk had to be read in full before the first byte arrived
An even spread of load for small popular files, since each lived on only three chunkservers
items.why: A small file is one chunk with three copies. When many clients read it at once those three machines are swamped. Disk space was not wasted, because a chunk file is only as large as its data.

items.ask: Why did the GFS master not log where each chunk's copies were stored?
choices: The chunkservers know what they hold and report it at startup and in heartbeats
Chunk locations change so often that logging them would fill the operation log within minutes
The locations follow from the chunk handle by a hash
items.why: Each chunkserver is the authority on its own disks. Asking them avoids keeping two records in step, and a chunkserver that fails or loses a disk simply stops reporting those chunks.

items.ask: By 2009, what set the limit on the GFS master's memory?
choices: The total bytes stored, since every byte of file data was also held in the master's memory as a cache
The number of files, since each file's metadata sat in memory
The bandwidth of the master's network link
items.why: Every file costs the master memory for its name and chunk list, so many small files cost far more than a few large ones holding the same bytes. The master never held file data, and its link carried only metadata.

items.ask: A team is building a storage system for large log files read by batch jobs. Which first design does GFS's history argue for?
choices: Distributed metadata from the start, since one coordinator always becomes the limit
One coordinator, with the limits it will hit written down
No coordinator: clients hash names to pick machines
items.why: A single coordinator makes global decisions simple and lasts as long as its load and memory stay small, which can be computed in advance. GFS carried Google for most of a decade before Colossus spread the metadata.

authors.title: The authors
authors.text: Ghemawat went on to build MapReduce (Lesson 8) and Bigtable (Lesson 10) with Jeff Dean, and later LevelDB. The paper appeared at SOSP, the Symposium on Operating Systems Principles, in 2003.

cache.title: Asking ahead
cache.text: A client usually asks for several chunks in one request, the one it needs and the next few, and the master answers with all their locations. A streaming reader may talk to the master only once every few hundred megabytes.

hotspot.title: The program everyone started
hotspot.text: The paper describes a batch queue that wrote a program into GFS as a single-chunk file and then started it on hundreds of machines at once. The few chunkservers holding it were overloaded; the fix was to store such programs with more copies and to stagger the starts.

colossus.title: What is known of Colossus
colossus.text: Google has published little about Colossus. A 2021 Google Cloud post described its metadata servers, which it called curators, keeping the file system's metadata in Bigtable, with the bytes on separate storage servers as in GFS. Bigtable in turn stores its own data in Colossus; the cycle is broken by a small, older store for the metadata of the metadata.

quinlan.title: Evolution on fast-forward
quinlan.text: Quinlan said the single master had been a deliberate shortcut to get something working quickly, and that by 2009 Google was running several masters per cluster over different parts of the namespace as a stopgap while the replacement was built.
